question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
